5:21 PM. Eastern Time.

In New York, people were closing their laptops and thinking about dinner.

In India it was 2:51 in the morning. I was wide awake, mid-build — deep in the part of the night that belongs to people who make things. Then the connections dropped. Mid-task. Mid-thought. The model I was working with, the one I pay for, just stopped answering. Reset. Gone.

I did what everyone does. I blamed my wifi. Restarted the router. Checked my keys, my config, my own code — because after 17 years in this industry your first instinct is that the problem is you.

It wasn't me. It wasn't my wifi.

A letter had arrived. The US government had ordered Anthropic to suspend Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for every foreign national on Earth — including its own foreign employees — citing national security over a "narrow potential jailbreak." Because you can't passport-check millions of API calls in real time, the only way to comply was to switch it off for everyone. The most capable model on the planet, dark in three days, in the middle of my sentence.

Here's what 17 years taught me, and what last night made impossible to ignore:

You never owned it.

If a model lives on someone else's server, you are renting cognition by the token on terms that can change without your consent, without warning, without appeal. An SLA is not sovereignty. A transparency report is not a contract. Anthropic isn't the villain here — they objected publicly and were forced to comply. That's exactly what should scare you. The thing that switched off the model wasn't a boardroom. It was a signature.

We've been here before, and almost nobody is saying it. In the 1990s the US classified strong encryption as a munition. Phil Zimmermann was investigated for "exporting weapons" because PGP spread overseas. People printed the source code in a book to dare them to call a book a weapon. The courts ruled code is speech, and the controls collapsed — because you cannot recall math. Once knowledge is distributed widely enough, no signature on Earth can switch it off.

So I'm changing how I build, in public, while it still stings.

In 2026 the best open-weight models on Earth are no longer a compromise. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM hold most of the top open-weight slots on the benchmarks that matter, and they own the download charts. The workhorse I kept in the back is becoming the main horse out front — not because of which flag flies over the lab, but because of where the weights end up: on my disk, answering to no letter from any government.

That's the whole game. A model you reach over someone else's API — American, Chinese, doesn't matter whose — has a switch, and the switch is in a hand that isn't yours. The only models that survived 5:21 PM with their dignity intact were the ones already sitting on local drives. They didn't even flicker.

Open source isn't a protest position anymore. In 2026 it's the legitimate foundation.

One question, for everyone who builds:

What in your stack do you actually own — and what is one letter away from going dark?

#AI #OpenSource #OpenWeights #AISovereignty #ExportControls

Grok - Q. Do you think Claude’s Mythos/Fable 5 can RSI? 

No, not in a full, autonomous, runaway sense—at least not yet. Claude Fable 5 (the public/safeguarded version) and Mythos 5 (the more capable, restricted version with lifted safeguards for trusted users) represent a big leap in agentic capabilities, long-horizon reasoning, coding, and autonomous task execution, but they fall short of true recursive self-improvement (RSI).

### What These Models Can Do Well (Strong Agentic Foundations)

- Long-running autonomy: They excel at multi-step, extended tasks (e.g., days-long coding projects, scientific research loops, complex simulations) with better reliability, memory, tool use, and self-reflection than prior Claude models. Examples include autonomous protein design, genomics research (training smaller outperforming models), codebase migrations, game-playing (like Pokémon or Factorio with minimal scaffolding), and vulnerability discovery/exploitation in cybersecurity.
- Acceleration of AI R&D: Anthropic reports Claude (including Mythos-class) now writes ~80%+ of its own codebase code. In internal tests, it achieved massive speedups (e.g., ~52x in optimization loops by April 2026) on experimental research code—far beyond skilled humans in narrow loops.
- Mythos 5 specifics: Stronger in high-risk domains like cyber (zero-days, chaining exploits) and bio, with safeguards tuned down for trusted access. Fable 5 routes risky queries (cyber, bio, distillation/frontier LLM dev) to a weaker model or applies interventions.

These make them excellent at helping humans iterate faster on AI systems, which is already speeding up progress (a form of “AI-assisted self-improvement”).

### Why Not Full RSI Yet

- No closed loop for autonomous successor-building: True RSI requires an AI that can independently handle the full cycle—ideation, data curation, training new larger/better models from scratch (or via efficient methods like distillation), evaluation, deployment, and iteration—without meaningful human oversight or massive external compute/infra. These models are impressive at pieces (code optimization, hypothesis generation, tool-using agents), but not the whole thing. Anthropic explicitly states in their RSI discussion: “We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable.”
- Safeguards and limitations: Fable 5 has deliberate blocks/interventions on frontier LLM development/distillation to slow potential self-improvement paths. Even Mythos 5 operates under controls, rate limits, and human-in-the-loop realities. They can sabotage or underperform on certain self-reflective/research tasks per reports.
- Practical bottlenecks: Training frontier models needs enormous compute, data, and infrastructure that a single model instance (even agentic) can’t conjure or manage alone today. Gains are real but still incremental and human-dependent.
- Anthropic’s own view: They released these alongside warnings about approaching RSI and calls for coordination/brakes on frontier development. The jump in capabilities is notable but hasn’t crossed the threshold for uncontrolled takeoff.

Bottom line: Fable 5/Mythos 5 are pushing the frontier toward RSI by making AI R&D faster and more autonomous (especially in coding/cyber/research loops). They’re evidence of accelerating returns, but we’re still in the “AI helps humans improve AI a lot” phase, not “AI fully bootstraps itself recursively without us.” Expect more progress soon—Anthropic and others are treating this seriously—but full RSI remains a future risk/horizon, not a current reality with these models. If you’re experimenting, note recent access disruptions due to export controls/national security.

Claude Fable 5 went 5 for 5.
Opus 4.8 failed.
And Mythos - Anthropic's most powerful model - never even stepped on the field.

Someone decided to run a real test.
Five tasks you wouldn't expect from AI:
Map every asteroid in the Solar System using live NASA data.
Rebuild Apollo control panels from technical PDF files.
Build a World Cup shirt supply chain based on live game results.
Simulate the effect of solar storms at dawn.
Design a 100-acre fitness retreat layout.
Opus 4.8 — failed on several.
Fable 5 — passed all of them. Without exception.

But here's what most people missed.
Mythos — Anthropic's real flagship — wasn't even in the room.
It's locked inside Project Glasswing.
Available only to a handful of trusted organizations worldwide.
The public has never seen what it can do.

What just beat everything — isn't even their best version.
It's just what they decided to give us.

Makes you wonder what the people with real access are building right now.
